wave_family: surface wave (Rayleigh-type, time-harmonic free surface wave on a half-space)
constitutive_model: generalized thermoelasticity, homogeneous isotropic: Lord-Shulman (Sec. 2, relaxation time tau) and Green-Lindsay (Sec. 3, constants alpha and alpha*)
geometry: homogeneous isotropic thermoelastic half-space occupying x3 >= 0 in rectangular Cartesian axes x1, x2, x3; plane free surface at x3 = 0; no lateral boundaries
couplings: thermo-mechanical: elastic dilatation coupled to temperature through the modified heat conduction equation; thermal expansion enters the stress-strain-temperature relation
assumptions: small-amplitude linear theory; no body forces and no external heat supply; Helmholtz decomposition into Lame potentials; potentials must decay away from the free surface (positive real parts of alpha1, alpha2, alpha3); constant surface heat-transfer coefficient h
governing_formulation: LS: displacement equation (2.1), modified Fourier heat conduction (2.2) with relaxation time tau, stress relation (2.3); GL: equations (3.1)-(3.2) and stress (3.6); free-surface conditions sigma_3k = 0 and a radiation condition linking theta,3 to h*theta on x3 = 0 (2.10, sign ambiguous in the OCR); characteristic equation (2.24) for LS and (3.10) for GL
verification: reduction checks only: (2.24) with tau = 0 reproduces Carroll's classical thermoelasticity characteristic equation; with h = 0 it equals the Nayfeh and Nemat-Nasser plane surface wave equation; tau = 0 with epsilon = 0 gives the elastic Rayleigh equation (2.25); GL (3.10) with alpha = alpha* = 0 reduces to the classical thermoelastic equation and with epsilon = 0 to (2.25). No numerical or experimental comparison is performed here
parameters_and_units: symbols defined but no numerical values: lambda, mu Lame constants; k thermal conductivity; alpha coefficient of linear thermal expansion; c-epsilon specific heat at constant volume; tau relaxation time; h surface heat-transfer constant; epsilon thermoelastic coupling; alpha, alpha* GL constants with time dimension; c1, c2 isothermal dilatational and shear wave speeds
reported_result: representation theorem of Knowles extended to harmonically time-dependent surface waves in LS and GL generalized thermoelasticity; the two characteristic equations (2.24) and (3.10) differ in general; if alpha = alpha* = tau the Rayleigh surface wave speed is the same in both theories; displacements follow from a single scalar potential (2.27)
limitations: analytic note only, no numerical or experimental results; the GL constants alpha and alpha* are given no relaxation-time interpretation; scanned PDF whose OCR text layer mangles most equations, so equations were read but not re-derived; conclusions rest on the assumed exponential decay of the potentials
sources: Agarwal V.K. (1978) Journal of Elasticity 8(2):171-177; DOI 10.1007/BF00052480 (DOI not printed in the PDF; matched from title, authors, journal and filename)
reproducibility: equations only; no data tables and no computer code; closed-form characteristic equations (2.24), (2.25) and (3.10) are stated in full

wave_family: surface wave (Rayleigh wave, two-dimensional motion in the x-z plane with zero y-displacement)
constitutive_model: generalized thermoelasticity, homogeneous isotropic: classical dynamical coupled (CD), Lord-Shulman (LS) and Green-Lindsay (GL) selected by relaxation times tau0, tau1 and switch delta
geometry: homogeneous isotropic thermoelastic half-space with plane boundary z = 0 and positive z-axis inside the solid; propagation along x; all fields independent of y
couplings: thermo-mechanical: dilatational (P) wave coupled to the thermal field while the shear (SV) wave remains unaffected; thermal expansion in the constitutive relation
assumptions: small-amplitude plane wave motion; heat sources, external forces and body forces absent; Lame potentials with vector potential along y; surface wave decay enforced by setting constants A2, A4 and A6 to zero; thermally insulated surface
governing_formulation: motion equation (1), heat conduction (2) with tau0, tau1 and delta, constitutive (3) and strain (4); potentials (6); ordinary differential equations (11)-(13); boundary conditions sigma_zz = sigma_xz = dT/dz = 0 at z = 0 (29); dispersion equation (31); polynomial Z^6 - 8Z^4 + 8(3-gamma)Z^2 - 8(2-gamma) = 0 (32) with Z = c_R/c2 and gamma from (34)
verification: frequency equation (31) reduces to the Nayfeh and Nemat-Nasser LS result when the two relaxation times are equal; CD theory is recovered as tau0 and tau1 tend to zero; the text states reduction to Lockett and to Nayfeh-Nasser under appropriate conditions; numerical CD/LS/GL curves are compared with each other. No experimental validation
parameters_and_units: sandstone: rho = 2.3 g/cm3; lambda = mu = 0.8e11 dyn/cm2; k = 0.6e-2 cal/(cm s C); epsilon = 0.073; alpha_t = 0.4e-5/C; c-epsilon = 0.23 cal/(g C); tau0 and tau1 of order 1e-13 s; dimensionless tau0 = 1, 5, 10 with tau1 = n*tau0, n = 0,1,2,3; Poisson ratio 0 < nu < 0.5; lambda = mu assumed so c1^2 = 3c2^2
reported_result: dispersion equation (31) depends on wave number, so generalized thermoelastic Rayleigh waves are dispersive and attenuated unlike the pure elastic case; Z^2 = (c_R/c2)^2 increases monotonically with Poisson ratio; differences between CD, LS and GL are clear as nu tends to 0 and vanish as nu tends to 0.5; amplitudes of u*, sigma_xx and T* start at unity and decay with depth kz
limitations: two-dimensional formulation with uy = 0; only a thermally insulated surface is treated; a single material (sandstone) with lambda = mu; results are presented graphically without tabulated values or error bounds; the m2 root is represented by its real part in the numerical work
sources: Abd-Alla A.N., Al-Dawy A.A.S. (2001) Journal of Thermal Stresses 24(4):367-382; DOI 10.1080/01495730151078171 (printed on page 1)
reproducibility: equations, a material data list and figures; no tabulated numerical results and no code

wave_family: surface wave (Rayleigh-type, inhomogeneous attenuated wave in the sagittal plane, x-z motion)
constitutive_model: generalized thermoelasticity, homogeneous isotropic, with constitutive (2) covering Lord-Shulman (epsilon = 1) and Green-Lindsay (epsilon = 0)
geometry: thermoelastic half-space occupying z > 0 with plane stress-free surface z = 0; wave motion restricted to the x-z plane and independent of y
couplings: thermo-mechanical: two coupled complex dilatational waves (qP and qT) plus an uncoupled shear wave with real velocity beta
assumptions: small-amplitude linear thermoelasticity; no body forces and no thermal sources; Helmholtz resolution of the displacement; thermal relaxation times restricted by tau1 >= tau0 >= 0; isothermal surface; decay of the wave field with depth (positive imaginary parts of q_j/c)
governing_formulation: balance equations (1), constitutive (2), Helmholtz resolution (5)-(8); biquadratic (12) for the two complex dilatational velocities; potentials (16); isothermal boundary conditions sigma_zz = 0, sigma_zx = 0, T = 0 at z = 0 (17); irrational dispersion equation (18); rationalized degree-7 polynomial (19) in h = c^2/beta^2
verification: the paper demonstrates reduction only: with eta = 0 and Gamma_11 = 1 equation (18) reduces to (2-h)^2 = -4 q1 q3, the classical elastic Rayleigh secular equation; spurious roots introduced by rationalization are identified by re-substitution into (18); roots are then filtered by the radiation condition. No experimental or independent numerical comparison
parameters_and_units: copper: thermal conductivity kappa = 40, 400, 2000 W/(m K); Ce = 383 J/(kg K); beta_T = 4e-5, 2e-4, 1e-3 /K; angular frequency omega = 2*pi*2n kHz; propagation velocity V in m/s; Q^-1 dimensionless
reported_result: dispersive attenuated Rayleigh wave at the isothermal surface: velocity decreases and attenuation increases with frequency; for MHz to GHz waves velocity falls and attenuation rises with thermal conductivity; sensitivity to specific heat decreases with frequency; velocity and attenuation both increase with thermal expansion; only one root satisfies the radiation condition
limitations: a true surface wave with real velocity is stated to be impossible in this model because beta is real, so all solutions are inhomogeneous attenuated waves; only one admissible root; a single material (copper) is used; results are graphical with no error bounds; the model is reported as not dissipative enough to produce additional Rayleigh waves
sources: Sharma M.D. (2014) Journal of Seismology 18:61-79; DOI 10.1007/s10950-013-9401-4
reproducibility: complete coefficient definitions for the degree-7 polynomial, material data and figures; no code and no tabulated numerical values

wave_family: surface wave (Rayleigh-type, inhomogeneous attenuated wave at a thermally insulated boundary)
constitutive_model: generalized thermoelasticity, homogeneous isotropic, with constitutive (2) covering Lord-Shulman (epsilon = 1) and Green-Lindsay (epsilon = 0)
geometry: thermoelastic half-space z > 0 with plane thermally insulated surface z = 0; x-z plane motion independent of y
couplings: thermo-mechanical: qP and qT dilatational waves coupled through the temperature field; shear wave propagates without decay
assumptions: small-amplitude linear thermoelasticity; no body forces or thermal sources; tau1 >= tau0 >= 0; insulated boundary expressed as vanishing normal temperature gradient; decay of the wave field with depth required for admissible roots
governing_formulation: isothermal-type balance equations (1)-(2) with Helmholtz resolution; boundary conditions sigma_zz = 0, sigma_zx = 0, dT/dz = 0 at z = 0 (20); irrational dispersion equation (21); three squarings give a degree-9 polynomial (22) in h = c^2/beta^2
verification: reduction check only: with eta = 0 and Gamma_11 = 1 equation (21) reduces to the classical elastic Rayleigh dispersion equation; the nine roots of (22) are tested against the original equation (21) to remove spurious roots, then filtered for decay with depth. No experimental or independent numerical comparison
parameters_and_units: limestone: lambda = 17 GPa; mu = 14 GPa; rho = 2600 kg/m3; kappa = 100 W/(m K); Ce = 960 J/(kg K); beta_T = 6e-6 /K; T0 = 300 K; tau0 = 1.0e-8 s; tau1 = 2.0e-8 s; frequency range 1 kHz to 1 GHz; particle motion sampled at kRz = 0, 0.5, 2, 5
reported_result: at the insulated surface velocity increases with thermal conductivity, the opposite of the isothermal case, and sensitivity to conductivity grows with frequency; particle motion may be rectilinear rather than elliptic and polarization is tilted at all depths; insulation can further reduce the speed and raise the attenuation substantially
limitations: single limestone example; results are graphical without reported tolerances; rationalization to degree 9 relies on squaring, and root acceptance depends on the numerical test against (21); no experimental data
sources: Sharma M.D. (2014) Journal of Seismology 18:61-79; DOI 10.1007/s10950-013-9401-4
reproducibility: coefficient definitions A0-A5 and B0-B4 for the degree-9 polynomial, material data and figures; no code and no tabulated numerical values

wave_family: surface wave (Bleustein-Gulyaev, shear-horizontal anti-plane surface wave)
constitutive_model: linear piezoelectricity of a 6 mm (hexagonal) crystal in the quasi-electrostatic approximation, functionally graded so that c44, e15, epsilon11 and rho all vary in the same proportion
geometry: half-space x2 >= 0 of a 6 mm piezoelectric functionally graded material; wave propagating along x1; symmetry axis along x3; sagittal plane normal to a binary axis; free surface at x2 = 0
couplings: piezoelectric: the anti-plane mechanical displacement u3 is coupled to the electric potential phi through the piezoelectric constant e15; anti-plane motion decouples from in-plane motion
assumptions: anti-plane shear-horizontal motion; quasi-static electric field with vacuum permittivity outside; single inhomogeneity function f(x2) with f(0) = 1 shared by c44, e15, epsilon11 and rho, which the authors call a strong assumption; subsonic speed interval (3.12)
governing_formulation: piezoacoustic equations (2.3) and first-order system (2.4) with matrices N2 and K; decoupled second-order system (3.3); exact evanescent solution (3.7); boundary conditions t23(0) = 0 with metalized phi(0) = 0 or free d2(0) = ik*epsilon0*phi(0); dispersion equations (3.15) metalized and (3.17) free, with alternative forms (3.20)-(3.21)
verification: analytic reduction checks: (3.20) and (3.21) coincide with (3.15) and (3.17) for the exponential profile P0, and both reduce to the classical homogeneous Bleustein-Gulyaev results (3.16) and (3.18) when beta = 0; equations (4.9) and (4.10) likewise reduce to (3.16) and (3.18) at beta = 0. No experimental or independent numerical comparison
parameters_and_units: PZT-4 at the interface: c44 = 2.56e10 N/m2; e15 = 12.7 C/m2; epsilon11 = 650e-11 F/m; rho = 7500 kg/m3; epsilon0 = 8.854e-12 F/m; homogeneous speeds v_m = 2256.85 m/s and v_f = 2592.65 m/s; K^2_S = 0.242; beta/k from 0 to 0.2 for the exponential and inverse quadratic profiles and 0 to 2 for the tanh profile; tanh(delta) = 1/sqrt(1.1)
reported_result: exact Bleustein-Gulyaev solutions exist for profiles P0-P10 plus a tanh^2 profile and a family (beta*x2 + 1)^(2p); for the decreasing exponential profile the free-surface speed is nearly unchanged while the metalized-surface speed falls, raising K^2_S from 0.242 to 0.324; the inverse quadratic profile gives 0.310; the asymptotically homogeneous tanh profile gives a metalized speed above the homogeneous value and a smaller K^2_S; v_f > v_m always so the wave penetrates deeper when the surface is not metalized
limitations: exactness is restricted to the listed inhomogeneity profiles and to the subsonic interval (3.12); profiles P0-P5 either blow up or vanish as x2 tends to infinity so near-surface localization must be assumed; the equal-proportion grading of rho with the other constants is acknowledged as physically strong; no experiments
sources: Collet B., Destrade M., Maugin G.A. (2006) European Journal of Mechanics A/Solids 25:695-706; DOI 10.1016/j.euromechsol.2006.01.007 (diacritics removed)
reproducibility: closed-form dispersion equations, Table 1 of inhomogeneity profiles, and speeds and coupling coefficients quoted in the text; no code and no digitized curve data

wave_family: guided wave (Lamb-type in a plate, including propagating, purely imaginary and complex evanescent branches)
constitutive_model: magneto-electro-elastic (piezoelectric-piezomagnetic) orthotropic functionally graded material with z-direction polarization; Voigt-type graded mixture of CoFe2O4 and Ba2TiO3
geometry: infinite plate of thickness h occupying 0 <= z <= h; wave propagating along x; upper and lower surfaces at z = 0 and z = h traction free
couplings: full magneto-electromechanical coupling: stress depends on elastic, piezoelectric and piezomagnetic terms, while electric displacement and magnetic induction depend on strain, electric field and magnetic field
assumptions: small-amplitude linear theory; material parameters fitted as power series in z/h; Voigt-type effective properties from volume fractions; boundary conditions embedded through a rectangular window function whose derivative gives Dirac deltas; traction-free surfaces with open or shorted electric and magnetic circuits
governing_formulation: field equations (1), constitutive relations (2), strain-electric-magnetic definitions (3); harmonic ansatz (4); property expansions (5)-(6); coupled governing equations (7a)-(7d) for U, W, X, Y; Legendre polynomial expansion (8)-(9); matrix equation (11) recast as the eigenvalue problem in k (14)-(15); conditions sigma_zz = sigma_xz = sigma_yz = 0 at z = 0,h with D_z = B_z = 0 (open) or phi = psi = 0 (shorted)
verification: comparison with published results: the full Lamb spectrum of a steel plate is compared with a spectral collocation method (Figure 2) and an orthotropic PZT-4 plate with a reverberation-ray matrix method (Figure 3), with good agreement reported; convergence with truncation order is documented in Figure 4 and Table 3, and M = 30 is adopted
parameters_and_units: h = 1 mm; CoFe2O4 and Ba2TiO3 constants in Table 1 (C_ij in 1e9 N/m2, epsilon_ij in 1e-10 F/m, e_ij in C/m2, q_ij in N/(A m), mu_ij in 1e-6 N s2/C2, rho in 1e3 kg/m3); steel verification rho = 7932 kg/m3, C11 = 281.757 GPa, C12 = 113.161 GPa, C44 = 84.298 GPa, h = 10 mm; dimensionless Omega = omega*h*sqrt(rho/C44)/pi and Psi = k*h/pi
reported_result: the eigenvalue formulation yields the complete real, purely imaginary and complex spectrum; at Omega = 0.1 the first complex wave number is 0.31308 + 0.67653i and is unchanged from M = 10 to M = 20; evanescent-mode phase velocity grows and attenuation falls with frequency and exceeds the propagating-mode velocity, e.g. the second evanescent mode is about 8 at fh = 2-3 against below 2 for the propagating mode; the magneto-electromechanical coupling factor K^2 peaks between 4.4 percent (sinusoidal graded field) and 9.5 percent (cubic graded field) near kh = 2 and kh = 1.5
limitations: semi-analytic truncated Legendre series: higher modes need larger M and hence more memory and time; convergence is demonstrated but no error bound is given; numerical results are specific to one material pair and h = 1 mm; no experimental data; the PDF text layer duplicates peer-review markup and required care when reading
sources: Zhang X., Li Z., Yu J. (2018) Materials 11:1186; DOI 10.3390/ma11071186
reproducibility: governing equations, material tables and a convergence table are provided; computations were implemented in Mathematica 8.0 but the code is not supplied

wave_family: guided wave (Lamb-like in a spherical curved plate, including non-propagating purely imaginary and complex branches)
constitutive_model: functionally graded piezoelectric material, orthotropic with polarization in the thickness direction; Voigt-type graded mixture of Ba2NaNb5O15 and PZT-4
geometry: spherical curved plate in spherical coordinates (r, theta, phi) with inner radius a, outer radius b, thickness h = b - a and radius-thickness ratio eta = b/h; wave propagating in the circumferential phi direction
couplings: piezoelectric: mechanical displacement coupled to the electric potential through the coupled Lamb-like system (7a), (7c), (7d); the independent SH equation (7b) is not analysed
assumptions: small-amplitude linear theory; material parameters fitted as power series f(r) = f(l)*(r/h)^l; orthotropic FGPM polarized along the thickness; traction-free or mechanically fixed surfaces at r = a and r = b; electric open circuit D_r = 0 or closed circuit phi = 0; only the Lamb-like coupled system is solved
governing_formulation: field equations (1), constitutive (2), strain and electric field (3); property expansions (4)-(5); harmonic ansatz (6); governing equations (7a)-(7d); Legendre expansion (8) over [a,b] with weighted residual integration giving matrix equation (9) and eigenvalue problem (12) for complex k; boundary conditions T_rr = T_rtheta = T_rphi = 0 or u_i = 0 at r = a,b with D_r = 0 or phi = 0
verification: two validation cases: a steel spherical plate with eta = 100 and h = 1 mm compared against Quintanilla et al. spectral collocation results (Figure 2), and an SH wave in a homogeneous GaAs piezoelectric plate compared against analytical literature results (Figure 3); convergence with M documented in Figure 4 and M = 30 adopted
parameters_and_units: FGPM examples use eta = 10 and a = 9 mm; Ba2NaNb5O15 and PZT-4 constants in Table 1 (C_ij in 1e10 N/m2, epsilon_ij in 1e-11 F/m2, e_ij in C/m, rho in 1e3 kg/m3); GaAs verification C11 = C22 = C33 = 118.8 GPa, C44 = 59.4 GPa, C12 = 53.8 GPa, e14 = 0.154 C/m, epsilon = 110.625e-12 F/m2, rho = 5307 kg/m3, h = 1 mm; dimensionless Psi = kh/pi and Omega = omega*h*sqrt(rho/C55)/pi
reported_result: complete three-dimensional spectrum: a finite number of real branches together with infinitely many purely imaginary and complex branches at any frequency, real and imaginary branches in opposite-sign pairs and complex ones in conjugate quadruples; non-propagating phase velocity increases with frequency and exceeds the propagating velocity, e.g. the fifth complex branch is above 6 at fh = 3-4 while real branches stay below 2; the electric circuit affects complex branches more than real ones and two propagating modes below the first cut-off disappear for a mechanically fixed surface; at Omega = 1.21019 the complex branch has Psi = 0.21937 - 0.02803i and at Omega = 1.21815 the real branch has Psi = 0.19264
limitations: only the Lamb-like coupled system is analysed, the independent SH equation is set aside; FGPM examples use a single radius-thickness ratio (eta = 10) and a = 9 mm; truncated Legendre series with no error bounds; no experimental validation; equations (1)-(2) in the PDF text layer are partly garbled
sources: Zhang X., Liang S., Han X., Li Z. (2018) Materials 11:2363; DOI 10.3390/ma11122363
reproducibility: governing equations, material tables and numerical eigenvalues quoted in the text; the Mathematica Eigenvalues routine is used but the code is not supplied
